Dear Sir or Madam,

Request for Internal Review — 26FOI 103 — response dated 22 September 2026
Requester: Sion Buckler

I request an internal review of the handling and substance of 26FOI 103.

This is an FOI review only. I am not asking the Wales Office to determine title, to reopen BP Properties Ltd v Buckler, or to adopt any party's case on the land. I am asking whether the letter of 22 September 2026 answered the request that was made, and whether the search described in it was adequate.

A. What is already on this file

1. 29 August 2026 — I asked the Wales Office for recorded information about Great House Farm. Your letter of 22 September quotes the request as five points. I adopt that quotation. The points were:

- records of any communication or outreach between Cadw, or its predecessor functions, and the Office of the Secretary of State for Wales / Welsh Office concerning Great House Farm during July–December 1988;
- records of any recommendation, briefing, submission, notification or formal appeal concerning the protection or listing of Great House Farm submitted to the Secretary of State;
- records of any communications with the occupiers and owners of the property before the refusal decision of 5 December 1988;
- any surviving destruction, disposal, transfer or accession documentation relating to the Great House Farm 1988 assessment file, including certificates, dockets, lists, database entries, retention schedules, disposal authorities or other contemporaneous records held by the Welsh Office, its predecessors, Cadw, or any repository to which relevant records were transferred;
- information regarding a decision made in relation to Great House Farm in 1988, including the evidence that was used to support that decision.

2. 8 September 2026 — acknowledgement from NIO FOI ([email redacted]), recording the request date as 29/08/26. It named no officer and described no search.

3. 22 September 2026 — covering email from the same NIO FOI mailbox, attaching “26FOI 103 - Buckler - Response.pdf”. The covering email contained no substance. The letter is signed Freedom of Information Team, Wales Office, and directs any review to [email redacted].

This review is within the two calendar months stated in that letter. The deadline you gave is 22 November 2026.

B. What the letter actually says, and what it does not

The operative paragraph is this:

“We have carried out a search of our digital records and have determined that the Wales Office does not hold the information requested. Any paper files previously held by the former Welsh Office relating to this matter would have been transferred to the National Assembly for Wales in 1999, and subsequently to the Welsh Government in 2007.”

That paragraph does not answer the request. The gaps are these.

1. Digital records only. The letter says a search of digital records. It does not say that paper, microfilm, card indexes, transfer lists, accession registers, or destruction schedules were searched. A 1988 Welsh Office file is a paper file. A search confined to current digital holdings cannot find it, and cannot find the transfer or destruction docket that the fourth bullet asked for.

2. “Would have been transferred” is not a search result. It is an assumption about devolution. It is not a statement that a transfer list was consulted, that a file for this house appears on that list, or that the file was received in Cardiff. “Would have been” covers three different outcomes: transferred, destroyed, or still here under another description. The letter does not distinguish them.

3. The fourth bullet asked for the transfer, disposal and accession records themselves. Those records, if they exist, are Wales Office records of what left the building. They are not the assessment file. Pointing me to the Welsh Government does not answer a request for the docket, the list, the database entry or the disposal authority. Those may still be held here even if the file went to Cardiff. The letter does not say they were searched for.

4. The five bullets are not answered one by one. There is no finding on communications with Cadw; no finding on any briefing or appeal to the Secretary of State; no finding on communications with occupiers and owners before 5 December 1988; no finding on the evidence said to have supported a 1988 decision. A single sentence that digital records do not hold “the information requested” does not show that each limb was searched.

5. The letter uses “the refusal decision of 5 December 1988” only because I used it. It does not say whether that decision is recognised, whether a file for it was identified, or whether the decision is one of the papers “which would have been transferred”. Silence on a dated decision is not a not-held finding.

6. “You may therefore wish” is not section 16 advice. Section 16 requires advice and assistance so far as reasonable. A reasonable step, where the department asserts a transfer, is to give the receiving body's file reference, the date of transfer, and the series. None is given. If the intention was section 21 (information reasonably accessible elsewhere), that exemption is not named, and the conditions are not addressed. A suggestion that I write to [email redacted] is not a section 21 notice.

7. “Does not hold” is stated as a conclusion. The search described cannot support it. A not-held finding under section 1 requires a search capable of finding the information. A search of digital records, plus an assumption about 1999, is not that search.

8. The request was answered from a Northern Ireland Office mailbox. The letter is in the name of the Wales Office. The review must be of the Wales Office search. Please confirm it will not be taken by the person who signed the 22 September letter.

C. What the reviewing officer is asked to determine

1. What was searched, by name: digital systems, paper series, transfer lists, accession registers, destruction schedules, Gwydyr House holdings, and any index of files passed to the National Assembly in 1999 or to the Welsh Government in 2007. If a location was not searched, say so.

2. For each of the five bullets, a separate finding: held, not held after the searches at (1), transferred (with date, recipient and reference), or destroyed (with date and disposal authority).

3. Whether any transfer, disposal or accession record relating to a Great House Farm 1988 assessment file is held by this department, as distinct from the assessment file itself.

4. Whether any record of a decision on or about 5 December 1988, or of communications with the occupiers or owners before that date, was identified even as an index entry.

5. If information is held and is not to be disclosed, a section 17 notice naming the exemption. Do not replace that notice with a referral.

6. If the review maintains that the file went to Cardiff, the transfer reference. Without it, the referral is an assertion.

D. Scope, so the review is not narrowed again

The window is July–December 1988. Possession of Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough, adjoining St Dochdwy's, was taken on 29 November 1988. Demolition of the farmhouse began on 6 December 1988. The refusal date in the request is 5 December 1988. Those dates fix the search. They do not ask you to decide the land.

I have made a parallel request to the Welsh Government, following the referral. That does not discharge 26FOI 103. A file can have been transferred and the transfer docket can still be here. Both questions were asked. Only one was gestured at.

E. Why these records are in scope, without asking you to decide title

The public index is https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/

The investigation distinguishes Parcel A (farmhouse, garden, buildings and yard — the family's maintained freehold interest out of the Bute estate) from Parcel B (eastern fields). Later papers use “whole farm”. BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 decided possession, limitation and the October 1974 letters. It did not decide the documentary root of Parcel A. Whether the Secretary of State or Cadw looked at this house in the week it was refused and pulled down is a records question. It is not a request that you adopt the family's case.

F. Preservation

Please preserve any record that may fall within 26FOI 103 while this review is open, including transfer lists, destruction schedules and anything due for routine disposal. Do not transfer or destroy in-scope material without a written receipt that can be disclosed on the review.

G. Reservation

This letter does not waive any position on title, registration, concealment, limitation, or any later reopening. It is an internal review under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. It is not a claim form and is not service of proceedings.

Please acknowledge receipt, give the review reference, and state the date by which the review will be completed. ICO guidance is that an internal review should normally be completed within 20 working days.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals
[email redacted]

*To each recipient separately, in your own capacity as a current or

This notice is addressed to each recipient *individually*. It is *not a
joint request*, and it does not ask any recipient to speak for, investigate
on behalf of, or answer in place of any other person or organisation. Each
recipient is asked to respond only in respect of records within that
recipient's own possession, custody or control, including records inherited
from a predecessor organisation or retained on its behalf.
1. Nature and purpose of this notice

This is a *formal preservation notice* concerning documentary material
relating to Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough-juxta-Penarth, adjoining
St Dochdwy's, and the subsequent development of the site, including the
area now associated with Church View Close.

It is *not a claim form, is not service of proceedings, and is not intended
to constitute or replace any FOI request, internal review, complaint,
subject-access request or other statutory process already made to any
recipient.*

The purpose of this notice is to require the preservation of potentially
relevant material while the documentary history, title chain, registration
history, planning history, possession proceedings, demolition and
subsequent development are being reconstructed.

A separate first-stage preservation notice has been issued or is being
issued to Cadw / Welsh Government FOI, HM Land Registry Wales Office and
DPO, Heneb / GGAT HER, RCAHMW, Vale of Glamorgan FOI Unit and DPO,
Glamorgan Archives, South Wales Police FOI, The National Archives, the
Wales Office FOI team, and the National Library of Wales. Persimmon Homes
(Wales) Ltd has received a separate preservation letter.

*You are receiving this notice separately because the published documentary
record places you, or a predecessor whose records may remain in your
custody or control, within the documentary, legal, professional,
administrative or development chain concerning this land.*
2. Land and documentary scope

Please preserve, and do not destroy, alter, overwrite, discard, transfer
out of custody without a recorded handover, or otherwise dispose of, any
record within your possession, custody or control relating to the land or
matters identified below.

The scope includes, without limitation, *originals, copies, working papers,
drafts, annotations, plans, photographs, negatives, films, tapes, maps,
registers, indexes, correspondence, emails and attachments, electronic

records, instructions, client or matter files, survey material and other
associated records.*

The 1877 split; the 1916 and 1939 tenancies; the 1938 Bute to Western
Ground Rents conveyance; the 1969 Western Ground Rents to BP Pension Trust
conveyance; and any plans, schedules, abstracts, searches, correspondence
or other documents relied upon in relation to those transactions.

*2. Possession proceedings and subsequent litigation*

The 1955 High Court and 1962 Cardiff County Court possession orders; the
1974 proceedings; *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2*; House of
Lords leave papers, including *YHL/PO/JO/10/11/2536*; and *Buckler v United
Kingdom (1989)*, including associated correspondence, instructions,
evidence, plans and working papers.

*3. Land registration*

The first registration of *WA231076*, including the application dated 30
November 1982; the first registration of *WA240304*, including the
application dated 23 February 1983; subsequent amalgamation, transfer or
closure; and every plan, conveyance, abstract, search, application,
correspondence trail or professional file relied upon in connection with
those registrations or changes.

*4. 1988 possession and demolition*

The taking of possession on or about *29 November 1988* and the demolition
commenced on or about *6 December 1988*, including any planning,
listed-building, heritage, police, enforcement, media, contractor, survey,
photographic or inter-agency liaison material.

*5. Planning and subsequent development, 1989–1996*

Planning application *89/01396/OUT*; reserved matters application
*92/00671/RES*; conditions 16–18; GGAT / Cotswold Archaeology material;
records concerning any *section 52, section 106, planning obligation, local
land charge or equivalent instrument*; and the transfer from BP to Ideal
Homes dated *3 December 1993*, together with all associated plans,
correspondence, approvals, agreements, searches and completion material.

*6. Family records*

Records concerning *Mary Doreen Williams (died 1983)* and *William Buckler*,
insofar as those records relate to Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, the land

registration, development or demolition.

*Loosemores of Cardiff; Robbins Olivey & Blake Lapthorn / Blake Morgan;

Thomas + Partners; Ideal Homes Wales; BP Properties; BP Pension Trust;

alteration or overwriting of potentially relevant material, including

information necessary to identify the transfer and its current location,

Dear Ms Applegate,

Thank you for your letter of 28 September 2026 acknowledging my emails of
26 and 27 September, and for allocating reference ICR/090/26. I note that
an investigation officer will contact me within ten working days.

I would like to place four further points on the file for the investigation
officer, in addition to those already set out in my emails.

1. Public record

Please treat https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/ as part of the
material already cited.

The landing page sets out, diagrammatically and with links to the
underlying evidence, the family’s case that Parcel A — the farmhouse,
garden and associated land on the Williams/Thomas line — was included
within a whole-farm registered title even though the documentary root by
which BP acquired that parcel remains unresolved.

Our paper title deed being stolen from our home resulting in us not able to
be present in court in 1974 (and so ownership adjudication was ajourned and
our ownership assertion was weakened (not exstiguished) we understand. But
the stretch of the imagine it takes to ever believe it was Western Ground
Rents or BPs is all based on absurdity after absurdity and does not in my
estimation, meet the criteria of what a sane, reasonable person would do.

The website greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com
deliberately distinguishes documentary records from family evidence,
reconstruction and unresolved inference. I am therefore not asking ICR to
accept every proposition on the site as established fact; I am asking that
the underlying records and the specific questions identified there be
considered.

2. Chronology now recorded by HM Land Registry

I had earlier written as if the two titles merged in 1983. That was wrong.
HM Land Registry’s letter of 23 March 2026 (Lisa Griffiths, ref N610CGV)
separates the first-registration events from the later amalgamation. My
correction of 27 September is already on your file.

The chronology that now matters is:

• 30 November 1982 — application to first-register WA231076.

• 23 February 1983 — application to first-register WA240304.

• 26 March 1983 — Mary Williams died. Our family’s account is that notice
of BP’s registration was received only after her death, during/ after that
mourning period. Whether that account can be established from the notice,
service and correspondence records is itself a question for investigation.

• 24 July 1986 — Hollis J. The historical title material still showed both
titles live.

• 2 February 1987 — an application to amalgamate the two titles was
recorded. WA240304 was subsequently closed and registration continued under
WA231076. This is the amalgamation event, distinct from the 1982/83 first
registrations. It occurred while the BP Properties Ltd v Buckler litigation
was still live and before the Court of Appeal judgment of 31 July 1987.

• *14 April 1989 — Buckler v United Kingdom was declared inadmissible by
the European Commission of Human Rights.*

I regard this as a further institutional failure that now requires
reconsideration. The decision treated BP as having rights in our land
parcel and referred to BP as the owners, although BP had been awarded
possession, not ownership, and ownership of Parcel A had never been
adjudicated in BP’s favour. The distinction is fundamental. Possession is
not the same thing as ownership, and an order for possession did not itself
determine that BP had acquired the underlying proprietary interest in
Parcel A.

On the family’s case, our ownership claim to Parcel A was never
extinguished. The question therefore is not simply whether BP obtained
possession through the proceedings, but whether any legal process ever
transferred, extinguished or superseded the family’s underlying proprietary
interest. If it did not, the basis upon which BP was subsequently treated
as having superior rights in the parcel requires examination.

That issue also goes directly to the later assertion that the family’s
occupation became “permissive” under BP’s 1974 licence letters. A party
cannot ordinarily confer a proprietary right it does not itself possess. If
BP did not own Parcel A, it is necessary to establish what legal interest
BP actually held that enabled it to grant my grandmother, or anyone else,
permissive occupation of that parcel — particularly where there had already
been a long succession of earlier attempts to establish a permissive basis
for the family’s occupation.
The point is especially significant because the person whose occupation was
supposedly made permissive was herself the long-standing occupier and, on
the family’s case, the superior title holder of the parcel, with the
family’s occupation extending back centuries. I therefore ask that the
investigation distinguish carefully between *possession awarded to BP,
ownership of Parcel A, and any alleged power to license the family’s
occupation*. Those are not interchangeable propositions, and the
documentary basis for treating them as such requires examination.

3. What I am asking ICR to review

HM Land Registry has told my MP, and said in its stage-two decision of 25
May 2026, that the title was registered correctly and that there is no
evidence of a mistake. That is the institutional position my family has
encountered for decades.

I am not asking ICR to determine title. I am asking whether that conclusion
was reached after a proper examination of the first-registration files and,
in particular:

• the documentary basis and extent claimed for Parcel A in the
first-registration applications;

• the missing 31 December 1969 conveyance and the 1971 abstract of title;

• the notice and service records, including what notice was given to the
occupier, when, and what effective opportunity existed to object;

• the three inconsistent closure dates now appearing in the HMLR record for
WA240304; and

• the 2 February 1987 amalgamation application, including what was actually
amalgamated, on what plans and documents, and what title information
existed at that point in the still-live litigation.

The concern is therefore not simply one of hindsight. Much of the relevant
material was created contemporaneously with the events in question. That is
why I raise mistake, concealment and procedural unfairness as matters
requiring investigation, rather than as findings I am asking you to make at
this acknowledgement stage.

4. Why the record was reconstructed from Y Wladfa

For almost two years I have been in the Welsh Settlement in Patagonia,
rebuilding a replica of the farmhouse in which I was born.

That reconstruction prompted me to revisit the documentary history of Great
House Farm and, in doing so, to compare the family evidence with the
surviving land-registration, court and archival records. That work is what
brought the title chronology and the unresolved Parcel A question back into
focus.

The replica is also a way of preserving the history of a house that was
demolished in December 1988. I mention this not as an argument on the
merits, but to explain why a historical record that had remained largely
unexamined for decades was reconstructed now, and why I have pursued the
underlying documents rather than relying solely on inherited family
accounts.

Y Wladfa itself exists because Michael D. Jones and those who followed him
judged that Welsh language, history, heritage, people, landscape and
buildings were being overwritten in Wales — the process they cited as the
work of a “decapitation committee”. Which makes it interesting 99% of UK
MPs refused to sign an EDM in 2025 condemning us Christians being
decapitated. Our land parcel was clearly a Christian stronghold and holy
sacred lands and we were clearly stewards of it for centuries.

The Patagonia Welsh settlement is where those things are instead kept,
celebrated and respected. The replica stands there for the same reason the
original house cannot stand on Parcel A.

I will wait to hear from the investigation officer.

I also take this opportunity to draw your attention to the enclosed PDF,
which contains photographs relating to a tree-planting ceremony on the
southernmost part of our claimed Parcel A and subsequent photographs
showing the tree being demolished. The ceremony is part of the family’s
evidence of its assertion of ownership: my great-grandfather is recorded as
planting the tree to commemorate that ownership. The photographs also
preserve contemporaneous visual evidence, including identifiable
individuals and machinery vehicle registration numbers, which may assist in
establishing who carried out the later destruction and in what
circumstances.

There is a further land-history issue which may be relevant to the wider
question of how our claimed parcel came to be treated as no longer
belonging to the family. The woodland to the north of our home, on our
claimed parcel, was taken at a time when my grandmother had undergone a leg
amputation in 1955 and had become wheelchair-bound. I understand that this
woodland was subsequently gifted to a charity, which has itself contacted
me recently; I enclose that correspondence with the present material.

Similarly, I understand that land to the south of the farmhouse was also
taken, notwithstanding that the 1955 possession order appears, on the
documentary material presently available to me, to have concerned the
parcel to the east of ours. The Council subsequently made the southern land
into a small green or park and, in the process, the commemorative tree and
other physical evidence of the family’s assertion of ownership were
destroyed. I appreciate that this moves beyond the immediate registration
question, but the destruction of physical evidence bearing directly upon
the family's historic claim may be relevant to understanding the subsequent
evidential position.

There is also a further matter which I mention cautiously because I do not
yet know its full significance. It has been alleged to me that the
long-serving Council Clerk for Llandough played a role in the destruction
of this evidence. When I initially raised the matter through FOI, his
response was, as I understand it, an attempt not to become involved. When
subsequently required to respond, he retired after approximately 35 years'
service. I am not asserting that these events establish misconduct or that
his retirement was connected with this matter; I do not presently know the
extent, if any, of the connection.

I include the material because I believe it may have evidential relevance,
whether to the immediate investigation or, if not, at a later stage when
the wider history of the land and the disappearance of evidence is
considered. The tree ceremony, its subsequent destruction, the photographs,
and the associated correspondence provide material evidence which I do not
think should be disregarded simply because some aspects of it may
ultimately fall outside the immediate scope of this review.

There is also an important cultural dimension to the evidence. The tree was
not merely a physical object: its planting appears to have been an act of
asserting and commemorating ownership according to the family’s
longstanding traditions and understanding of the land. I recognise that
questions of ancient custom and tradition may not fall within the immediate
legal scope of ICR/090/26. I mention them because the destruction of the
physical manifestation of that assertion removed evidence of the very claim
whose documentary survival is now being investigated.
